planting.note: Divide and pot offsets in spring into a gritty, mineral-rich succulent mix.

directions: Grow in bright filtered light or partial shade rather than harsh direct sun, which scorches the tightly packed, corrugated leaves. The sprawling stems branch and offset readily from the base, slowly forming a dense clump. Water moderately through the warm growing season, letting the mix dry fully between waterings, and keep nearly dry and cool through winter dormancy.

planting.note: Pot offsets in spring into lean, rocky, fast-draining succulent soil.

directions: Native to karroid flats of South Africa's Eastern Cape, this small succulent carries sharp-tipped, flat-triangular leaves arranged in tidy spiral rows along slender stems. It prefers some protection from intense sun, holding its deep green color best in bright but filtered light, and turning purplish if pushed into stronger exposure. Keep nearly dry in winter and water sparingly during the growing season; it produces small greenish-white flowers with green midribs from late winter into early fall.

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring; pot into extremely well-drained, low-fertility mix.

directions: This Little Karoo native grows on rocky shale ridges and favors semi-shade over full exposure in cultivation; dark margins and tubercles fade toward pinkish-white if grown too bright. Leaves are lighter green than related Astroloba species, with fine dark lines running the underside. From late spring into early fall it sends up slender, mostly unbranched flower stalks over a foot long bearing small tubular yellowish flowers. Keep soil extremely well-drained and water only sparingly year-round.

planting.note: Pot small clustered offsets into sandy, nutrient-poor, slightly acidic mix.

directions: Discovered clinging to cliff faces above the Buffels River in South Africa's Klein Karoo, this small clustering succulent naturally hangs pendant from rock walls at 600-800m elevation. Its blue-green leaves turn reddish-purple when grown in strong sun, so partial shade suits it best and keeps the cooler coloration seen in its shaded wild habitat. Plant in sandy, nutrient-poor soil and water only minimally throughout the year, letting the mix go fully dry between waterings.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in a fast-draining epiphyte mix; best in a hanging pot.

directions: Native to tropical and montane forests of Brazil and Argentina, this trailing epiphytic cactus grows naturally in the dappled, humid shade beneath the forest canopy rather than out in open sun. Flattened, serrated stem segments branch and cascade from the base, making it well suited to a hanging basket. Give it partial shade to full shade, high humidity, and a coarse, fast-draining mix, letting it dry slightly between waterings; it rewards good care with nodding, creamy-white, faintly yellow-tinged flowers that can appear repeatedly through the year.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in a rich but well-drained epiphyte mix; grow as a hanging or trailing specimen.

directions: This epiphytic or lithophytic forest cactus from Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay forms many-branched, trailing masses of slender green stems rather than growing as an upright, sun-hardened cactus. It is best grown in bright indirect light with only brief direct morning or late sun, reflecting its origin beneath subtropical forest canopy. Water regularly through the growing season, allowing partial drying between waterings and reducing water in winter; masses of small white flowers appear in spring.
